samples.question: Somewhere in this picture there is one small framed block, and every grey mark outside that block is inert decoration that changes nothing. Inside the block, at the top, stand two upright tanks side by side, a left tank and a right tank. Each tank is divided into six equal cells by thin pale lines, so each tank holds at most six cells of liquid, and the liquid always rests on the floor of its tank as a solid dark-teal column. The two tanks together always hold exactly six cells of liquid. Below the tanks, still inside the block, there are three pour instructions stacked one above another; they act in order from the top instruction to the bottom one. Each instruction is a thick orange arrow beside one, two or three small dark pips. The arrow points at the tank the liquid is poured into, so an arrow pointing right pours from the left tank into the right tank and an arrow pointing left pours from the right tank into the left tank. The pips say how many cells of liquid that pour asks for. A pour is saturating: it moves the number of cells the pips ask for, unless the tank it pours out of holds fewer cells than that, in which case it moves only the cells that are actually there and the rest of the request is lost. Liquid is never created or destroyed, and the colour of the liquid never changes. After all three pours have been applied in order, how many cells of liquid are in the left tank? Answer with one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
